title: Wildfires: Are We Ready for Next Summer?
label: 15 September 2026 · Wildfire readiness hearing
summary: The Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee questioned DEFRA and MHCLG Ministers and officials about the unprecedented 2026 wildfire season. They discussed what went wrong, the lack of a national strategy, poor cross-government coordination, the emergency alert, and practical measures like water availability and land management. The overall conclusion was that the current approach is not fit for the future, and urgent action is needed before next spring.

speakers.label: Baroness Blake of Leeds
speakers.name: Baroness Blake of Leeds
speakers.role: Minister for Building Safety, Fire and Resilience, MHCLG

speakers.label: Gabrielle Edwards
speakers.name: Gabrielle Edwards
speakers.role: Interim Director for Strategy, Governance and Climate, DEFRA

chapters.title: Lessons from a Record-Breaking Summer
chapters.takeaway: The 2026 wildfire season was unprecedented and the Government accepts that current plans are not fit for the future.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: This summer we saw record wildfires, 19 homes destroyed and over 50,000 acres burned. What lessons have you learned?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: This summer has changed everything. We had over 1,300 wildfires—record numbers. What we have in place now won't be fit for managing fires in 10 years' time. We need to look again at land management, responsiveness and behaviour change.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: Fire and wildfires is back in MHCLG, which is the right place. The response from the fire service was extraordinary. The real step change is the impact on urban fringes—homes and vital infrastructure threatened. We need to focus on prevention, mitigation, recovery and future preparedness.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: People in rural communities have lived with this for years. It took homes being destroyed in Stourbridge for the Prime Minister to convene Cobra. Is that what it takes?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: The wider public understanding of the risk is something we haven't seen before. The Prime Minister is committed to holding a wildfire summit in October, bringing together everyone involved, including community representatives.

chapters.title: A National Strategy?
chapters.takeaway: There is still no national wildfire strategy, but Ministers say they are working on an action plan and joint governance.

turns.speaker: Josh Newbury
turns.text: Why does England still not have a national wildfire strategy? Will you commit to publishing one before next season?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: I'm focused on a one, two and 10-year vision. We're increasing resources in DEFRA and working on an action plan. We need to be in a stronger place by spring next year, rather than just writing a strategy.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: We're working towards a strategy through the action plan, but we're not waiting for that to start co-ordinating. The joint governance between our Departments is essential. There's a level of co-ordination across Government that hasn't been there.

chapters.title: Aerial Firefighting and Equipment
chapters.takeaway: The UK lacks dedicated aerial firefighting assets, but the Government is looking at cost-effective options, including drones, for next summer.

turns.speaker: Sarah Bool
turns.text: The UK doesn't have a dedicated aerial firefighting capability. Is reliance on commercial providers sufficient?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: You're right to raise this; it's top of the agenda for the summit. Fire chiefs say aerial intervention is good at putting out flames but not the underlying fire. We're looking at all options.

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: We've always relied on fire services resourcing themselves. But 44 services competing for the same asset isn't cost-effective. We're talking to providers and looking at drones. We need to be in a much better place by next summer.

chapters.title: Planning, Water and Land Management
chapters.takeaway: Wildfire risk needs to be built into planning, water supply and land management, but there are tensions over controlled burning and reservoir planning.

turns.speaker: Charlie Dewhirst
turns.text: The 2026 planning framework requires developers to mitigate wildfire risk. What does that mean in practice?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: Simple measures like fire breaks can slow down fire spread and give the fire service time. It's about balancing design with basic protection.

turns.speaker: Sarah Dyke
turns.text: Water availability is a growing challenge. During the New Forest fires, maintaining water supply was difficult. Are you considering stronger requirements on water companies?

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: We need water resilience. There are legal duties on water companies for emergency preparedness. We're working with them and will take this away.

turns.speaker: Henry Tufnell
turns.text: Only two out of 24 licence applications for controlled burning were approved. Why so few?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: Most were for training, not wildfire mitigation. The fire service advised they could train elsewhere. We're talking to the CLA about making the process more flexible.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Are you determined to leave fire load on the hill?

turns.speaker: Gabrielle Edwards
turns.text: No, but if we want to re-wet the peatland, controlled burning works against that. We need a transition. If credible applications come in, we'll issue licences.

chapters.title: Emergency Alert and Risk Register
chapters.takeaway: The August emergency alert was requested by the fire service and deemed a success, but the national risk register needs updating to reflect the increased wildfire risk.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: The national alert on 14 August was a significant moment. Should it have been issued sooner? Was it a success?

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: There are different views, but on balance the benefit is recognised. We need sophisticated procedures. It caught the public's attention, though there were criticisms about vulnerable people and the Welsh language delay.

turns.speaker: Jenny Riddell-Carpenter
turns.text: The decision was taken on the advice of the fire service. Many people got multiple alerts due to poor signal—that's a real issue in rural areas. Overall, it was important.

turns.speaker: Terry Jermy
turns.text: The national risk register still says the reasonable worst-case wildfire scenario is remote, around 1%—less likely than a volcanic eruption. Is that accurate?

turns.speaker: Peter Lee
turns.text: That's a fair point. The risk has changed faster than expected. We had 11 major incidents on one day. We need to review the risk assessment and will do so before next season.

chapters.title: Final Urgency
chapters.takeaway: The Committee warns that time is short before the next wildfire season and urges Ministers to act with urgency.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: It's September now. We'll be into the next wildfire season before we know it. The machinery of government can grind slowly. It's your jobs to make sure it doesn't.

turns.speaker: Baroness Blake of Leeds
turns.text: I take that point. We're also looking carefully at the health and wellbeing needs of firefighters. It's critical that we look after the people who keep us safe.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: I agree: it's all about the people. That's all we have time for today. Thank you.
